# Agent instructions

Read the applicable shared Lunchbox Labs standards before editing this repository:

- [Common agent guidance](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/.github/blob/main/agent-guidance/common.md)
- [Workflow conventions](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/.github/blob/main/agent-guidance/workflows.md)
- [npm package conventions](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/.github/blob/main/agent-guidance/npm-packages.md)
- [Agent tooling conventions](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/.github/blob/main/agent-guidance/agent-tooling.md)
- [State machine conventions](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/.github/blob/main/agent-guidance/state-machines.md)

These documents must be read explicitly; GitHub does not automatically inherit them here.

This repository is an npm workspace with two published packages, released together at one version, and their private shared source:

- `packages/core`: `@lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-core`, private and never published. All shared logic, built for a host from a `Host` profile (the host's name in messages, access labels and access notes).
- `packages/opencode`: `@lunchbox-labs/opencode-tool-inspector`, the OpenCode adapter.
- `packages/kilo`: `@lunchbox-labs/kilo-tool-inspector`, the Kilo adapter.

Put behaviour in core and keep the adapters to their `Host` profile and entry point. Express host differences as profile data where you can. Core has no runtime dependency on any host package; it is typed against `@opencode-ai/plugin`, and the Kilo adapter adapts Kilo's API type to it. Each adapter's build (tsdown, `tsdown.config.ts` in the package) bundles core's source into one `dist/tui.js` and `dist/tui.d.ts` and keeps every other import external; it fails if anything from `node_modules` would be inlined. No adapter lists core in any dependency field. A runtime dependency added to core must also go into each adapter's `dependencies` and into `deps.onlyImport` in both `tsdown.config.ts` files, and the baseline and package tests that assert the adapters have no dependencies must be updated. Core resolves to its TypeScript source through the workspace link, so tests and typechecking need no build.

Run commands from the repository root. `npm run check` includes static checks and unit tests for every package. Run `npm run test:package` separately for packed-package validation, and `npm run test:native` (with `NATIVE_HOST=kilo` and `KILO_TEST_VERSION=floor` or `latest-compatible`) for the native Kilo TUI check.

Both host packages are TUI-only: they export `./tui` and no root or `./server` entry, because OpenCode and Kilo load a package's root export as a server plugin.

Each host package's `@opentui/*` and `solid-js` dev dependencies must stay on the versions its supported host bundles; `packages/opencode/tests/opencode-baseline.test.mjs` and `packages/kilo/tests/kilo-baseline.test.mjs` enforce this. Update them only together with the supported host range in that package's `tests/opencode.json` or `tests/kilo.json`. Core's host dev dependencies match the OpenCode package's.

The GitHub wiki is published from `docs/wiki/`: the Wiki workflow replaces the wiki with that folder on every push to `main` that changes it, so edit pages there, never in the wiki itself. Each file is one page named after its filename, with `_Sidebar.md` as the sidebar; link pages by name, as in `[Usage](Usage)`. Keep in-depth user and developer guides in the wiki and the README to a short introduction that links to them.

Write documentation for knowledgeable OpenCode and Kilo users: explain plugin-specific concepts without host or package-install basics or unnecessary cautions. Keep installation examples simple and unversioned. Keep maintainer publishing and release-process walkthroughs out of the README and user pages; the wiki's Developer pages hold them, and release notes are still appropriate.

The plugin's state machines are documented in [docs/state-machines.md](docs/state-machines.md). Update it in the same PR as any change to their states, triggers or exits, with tests for each transition and failure path the change adds or alters.

## Contributor workflows

Request an independent `opencode-user-review` for changes to tool listing, tool details, input editing, tool calls, diagnostics or user-facing documentation that OpenCode users see, and a `kilo-user-review` for those that Kilo users see; a change to core usually needs both. Unrelated changes do not need them. Give the reviewer the diff/base and relevant test or runtime evidence.

Use `.agents/skills/native-package-verification/SKILL.md` to select applicable package and host checks; it is not an additional review role. The [agent tooling conventions](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/.github/blob/main/agent-guidance/agent-tooling.md) cover the file layout, invocation in each tool and reviewer permissions.

# Tool Inspector

Browse the tools available to agents from the OpenCode or Kilo TUI: each tool's description, input schema and the agents that can use it.

| Host | Package |
| --- | --- |
| OpenCode | [`@lunchbox-labs/opencode-tool-inspector`](packages/opencode) |
| Kilo | [`@lunchbox-labs/kilo-tool-inspector`](packages/kilo) |

Both bundle the shared source in [packages/core](packages/core), which is not published. The [wiki](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/wiki) has the [usage](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/wiki/Usage) and [developer](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/wiki/Developer) guides.

# Tool Inspector core

Internal source shared by the [Tool Inspector](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin) host packages, `@lunchbox-labs/opencode-tool-inspector` and `@lunchbox-labs/kilo-tool-inspector`. It is private and never published: each host package's tsdown build bundles it at build time. Its API isn't stable.

The [Developer](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/wiki/Developer) wiki page describes the layout and build.

# Kilo Tool Inspector

Browse the tools available to Kilo agents from the TUI: each tool's description, input schema and the agents that can use it.

Requires Node **22.18+**. Built for Kilo CLI **7.8.x**, starting at **7.8.27**. For OpenCode, use [`@lunchbox-labs/opencode-tool-inspector`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@lunchbox-labs/opencode-tool-inspector).

## Install

Add the package to `plugin` in `tui.jsonc`:

```jsonc
{ "plugin": ["@lunchbox-labs/kilo-tool-inspector"] }
```

## Browse tools

Run `/tools`, or **Browse tools** from the command palette, to list the tools Kilo offers a model; the dialog's title names which one. Type to filter the list, press Enter to see a tool's input schema, the agents that can use it and its full description, and press Escape to return to the list.

A tool's detail shows each agent's configured access. Kilo can still ask or deny at call time, for example for protected config paths or exact `agent_manager` action rules, so the detail notes where that applies.

## Documentation

The [wiki](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/wiki) has the full guides for both hosts:

- [Usage](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/wiki/Usage): which model's tools are listed, what the list leaves out and how input schemas are shown.
- [Agent access](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/wiki/Usage#agent-access): how a tool's detail shows each agent's access.
- [Developer](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/wiki/Developer): development, compatibility testing and publishing.

# State machines

This document describes the state Tool Inspector keeps across commands, dialogs and host events. Update it in the same PR as any change to these states, their triggers or their exits, following the [state machine conventions](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/.github/blob/main/agent-guidance/state-machines.md), and cover each transition you add or change in the packages' `tests/` folders. Known bugs belong in issues, not here.

All of this state lives in the shared core, `packages/core/src/`, and is the same in OpenCode and Kilo. Each host package bundles core into its single `dist/tui.js` at build time, so this state exists once per loaded plugin, and builds the plugin with its own `Host` profile, which only changes wording: the host's name in messages and notices, the labels for allowed, asks-first and denied access, and any notes shown above a tool's agents. Kilo's profile adds a note that the access shown is from configured rules, a protected-config note for tools checked as `read` or `edit`, and an exact-action note for `agent_manager`.

The plugin keeps no kv-persisted state, no intervals and no retries. Its only deferred work is the detail view's focus timeout and the microtask that returns to the list.

## Browser dialog controller

`registerToolBrowser` in `packages/core/src/tui.ts` keeps `revision`, `showing` and `activeRead`, changed by `close`, `display`, `open`, `views.list`, `views.detail` and the `server.instance.disposed` watcher. Every displayed dialog gets a revision, and stale host close callbacks and late reads compare against it and do nothing. Each step takes a `sameView` check from `viewContext`, which holds while the directory, route and session are unchanged and the plugin lifecycle is not aborted.

- `/tools` or the palette's "Browse tools" opens a "Loading tools" alert and starts a catalog read, from any state. Running it during a read aborts the previous read.
- A read that resolves for the current revision and view shows the tool list, with one toast for any notices first. A failed read or an empty catalog closes with a toast. A read for a changed view closes without one.
- Escape, ctrl+c, Enter on the alert, a backdrop click or a host dialog replacing the alert calls its close callback, which aborts the read, and its late result is dropped. Plugin dispose also aborts the read, and the alert closes without a toast.
- Choosing a tool waits for the detail viewer and shows the detail for the same revision and view; if the view changed while it waited, nothing happens and the list stays. If building or showing the detail throws, a toast names the tool and the list stays. Choosing after the view changed closes with a toast to run `/tools` again.
- Closing the detail, including a host dialog replacing it, queues a microtask that reopens the list on the same tool when the revision is unchanged, no host dialog is open and the view is the same; otherwise the browser stays closed.
- `server.instance.disposed` for this directory closes any plugin dialog.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Idle
    Idle --> Loading: /tools or palette
    Loading --> Loading: /tools again, previous read aborted
    Loading --> List: read ok, same view, tools found, notices toasted
    Loading --> Idle: read failed or no tools, toast
    Loading --> Idle: view changed during the read
    Loading --> Idle: alert closed or replaced, read aborted
    Loading --> Idle: instance or plugin disposed
    List --> Loading: /tools
    Detail --> Loading: /tools
    List --> DetailPending: tool chosen, same view
    List --> Idle: tool chosen after the view changed, toast
    List --> Idle: closed, replaced or instance disposed
    DetailPending --> Detail: viewer ready, revision unchanged
    DetailPending --> List: detail failed, toast
    DetailPending --> List: view changed while waiting
    DetailPending --> Idle: list closed meanwhile
    Detail --> Returning: Escape, ctrl+c, backdrop or replaced by a host dialog
    Detail --> Idle: instance disposed
    Returning --> List: same revision, no dialog open, same view
    Returning --> Idle: host dialog open or view changed
```

## Detail viewer

`viewer` in `packages/core/src/tui.ts` memoizes the promise from `createDetailViewer` in `packages/core/src/detail-viewer.ts`, started by the first `/tools`. If importing `@opentui/core` fails, one warning toast says details show as plain text. Both the scrollable viewer and the plain-text fallback last for the plugin's lifetime.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Unloaded
    Unloaded --> Loading: first /tools
    Loading --> Ready: import ok
    Loading --> PlainText: import failed, one toast
    Ready --> [*]: plugin disposed
    PlainText --> [*]: plugin disposed
```

## Catalog read

Each `/tools` read in `packages/core/src/tui.ts` collects `modelFailure`, `listFailure` and `agentsFailure` while `agentsRead` runs in parallel.

- `chooseModel` takes the model of the session's latest user message, then the configured `model` when its provider is connected or no provider is listed, then the default of the first connected provider that has one, then none. A failed providers request is kept as `modelFailure`.
- The tool list comes from `tool.list` for that model. If it fails, returns the wrong shape or there is no model, it falls back to `tool.ids` with names only and a notice. If `tool.ids` errors or returns the wrong shape too, the read fails.
- `readAgents` and `accessByTool` add each tool's agent access. If they fail, the detail leaves out its Agents section and a notice says why.

Every degraded outcome carries a notice, which the controller toasts.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ResolveModel
    ResolveModel --> ToolList: session, configured or provider default model
    ResolveModel --> IdsFallback: no model found or providers request failed
    ToolList --> Full: tool.list ok
    ToolList --> IdsFallback: tool.list error or wrong shape
    IdsFallback --> NamesOnly: tool.ids ok, notice
    IdsFallback --> Failed: tool.ids error or wrong shape
    Full --> JoinAgents
    NamesOnly --> JoinAgents
    JoinAgents --> WithAgents: agents read
    JoinAgents --> WithoutAgents: agents failed, notice
    Failed --> [*]
    WithAgents --> [*]
    WithoutAgents --> [*]
```

## Detail view instance

Each render from `createDetailViewer` creates a scroll view, waits 1 ms to focus it and activate its paging keymap layer, and refits on resize. When the host removes the dialog, or the plugin aborts, it is destroyed and clears its focus timer, resize listener, keymap layer and abort listener.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Created: render
    Created --> Focused: 1 ms timer, not destroyed or aborted
    Created --> Destroyed: removed before the timer
    Focused --> Focused: paging keys, resize
    Focused --> Destroyed: dialog removed or plugin aborted
    Destroyed --> [*]
```

## Schema rendering

`schemaLines` in `packages/core/src/schema-text.ts` renders a tool's input schema each time its detail opens, synchronously, keeping a `Rendering` for that call: the lines written, the remaining character and reference-lookup budgets, how often a depth limit cut a listing short, the `allOf` merges that left members out, where each shared definition's fields were listed, and the first field that refers to each definition.

- A missing or non-object schema says the host reported no input schema.
- Fields are written one line at a time. A line over 400 characters ends in "…", and enum, union, `type` and tuple element lists name their first few values and count the rest. Tuples read their elements from `prefixItems`, or an `items` list, and any further elements from `items` or `additionalItems`. Listings go 9 levels deep (depths 0 to 8) and write a "…" line below that, and array items, unions and `allOf` members are followed at most 64 levels, with "…" where `allOf` members were left out.
- Writing a 401st line, or going over 100,000 characters or 50,000 reference lookups, throws `SchemaTooLarge`. If lines were written they end with "… Schema too large to show in full."; otherwise the raw schema shows, cut to 400 lines with a count of the rest. Any other error, such as a stack overflow, also shows the raw schema.
- A root union lists each option's fields, under the same limits as any listing. A root with no fields to list shows `Input is <type>`, "Takes no input." or, for combinators that can't be listed, the raw schema.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NoSchema: schema missing or not an object
    [*] --> Listing: detail opened
    Listing --> Listed: fields or a root union's options written within the limits
    Listing --> Summary: no fields, only a type or no input
    Listing --> CutShort: line, character or lookup limit after lines were written
    Listing --> RawSchema: limit before any line, unlistable combinators or another error
    NoSchema --> [*]
    Listed --> [*]
    Summary --> [*]
    CutShort --> [*]
    RawSchema --> [*]
```

### References

Each `$ref` resolves to one of four outcomes. A reference that misses under `#/$defs/` or `#/definitions/` is retried under the other, since OpenCode 1.19 and Kilo 7.8 rename zod's `$defs` without rewriting references, and references are keyed by the spelling that resolved. A definition that is only a reference to another is followed.

- **Resolved:** the target, with the reference's own keys over it, is rendered and the reference joins the set being expanded.
- **Recursive:** the target is already being expanded. Its type is the definition's name, or for a generated name such as zod's `__schema0`, its own type, else "same type as <field>" for the first field that refers to it, else "recursive value". A field that refers back says "Same fields as <path>." where that definition is being listed.
- **Unresolved:** the reference isn't local or names nothing under either spelling. A node with no other type shows "unresolved reference <name>".
- **Chain too long:** more than 64 references in a row. A node with no other type shows "reference chain too long".

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Following: node has a $ref
    Following --> Following: target is only a reference to another
    Following --> Resolved: target found, not being expanded
    Following --> Recursive: target already being expanded
    Following --> Unresolved: not local, or missing under $defs and definitions
    Following --> ChainTooLong: more than 64 references in a row
    Resolved --> [*]
    Recursive --> [*]
    Unresolved --> [*]
    ChainTooLong --> [*]
```

### Shared definitions

Within one rendering, each shared definition is listed once. A use that lists fields records its path and depth before writing them, so references back into it from inside can name it, then records whether a depth limit cut it; if it wrote nothing, the earlier record is restored. A later use says "Same fields as <path>." unless the recorded listing was cut and the use is shallower, in which case it lists the fields again and replaces the record. A use with its own shape beside the `$ref`, such as extra properties, always lists in full.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Unlisted
    Unlisted --> Listing: first use with fields
    Listing --> Unlisted: listing wrote nothing
    Listing --> Complete: listed within the depth limits
    Listing --> Cut: listing cut by a depth limit
    Listing --> Listing: reference back from inside, "Same fields as" its path
    Complete --> Complete: later use refers to it
    Cut --> Cut: use at the same depth or deeper refers to it
    Cut --> Listing: shallower use lists it again
```

## Registration and minor state

- The plugin registers its keymap layer and a `server.instance.disposed` subscription, and removes both on `api.lifecycle.onDispose`. Dispose aborts a pending read, which closes the loading alert. It does not close a list or detail: the detail view destroys itself on abort, and a list left open answers Enter with the toast to run `/tools` again.
- `compiledWildcards` in `packages/core/src/agents.ts` memoizes one regular expression per permission pattern for the process.
- `literalTexts` in `packages/core/src/schema-text.ts` is a WeakMap that caches a const or default's shortened text by object identity, across renderings. It is never invalidated, so a schema object the host changes in place keeps its old literal text until it is replaced.
- The host owns the list's filter and cursor. Returning from a detail restores the cursor on the tool, but not the typed filter.

---
name: kilo-user-review
description: Use when changes affect tool listing, tool details, input editing, tool calls, diagnostics or user-facing documentation that Kilo users see.

# Developer documentation

For contributors and maintainers working on Tool Inspector:

- [Workspace layout](#workspace-layout): the host packages and their shared core.
- [Local builds and checks](#build-local-packages): local builds, the TUI-only package shape and compatibility checks for each host.
- [Publishing](Publishing): trusted publisher setup and the release workflow.

The plugin's state machines are documented in [docs/state-machines.md](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/blob/main/docs/state-machines.md). These wiki pages are published from [docs/wiki](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/tree/main/docs/wiki) on every push to `main` that changes them; change them there.

The repository's [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/blob/main/AGENTS.md) and linked shared standards remain the authoritative machine instructions. [User documentation](Home#user-documentation) covers installation and everyday use.

## Workspace layout

The repository is an npm workspace with one lockfile. Its two host packages share one version and are released together. Core is private: it is never published, and each host package's build bundles it in.

| Directory | Package | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `packages/core` | `@lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-core` (private) | All shared logic, and the `Host` profile type |
| `packages/opencode` | `@lunchbox-labs/opencode-tool-inspector` | OpenCode's `Host` profile and `./tui` entry |
| `packages/kilo` | `@lunchbox-labs/kilo-tool-inspector` | Kilo's `Host` profile and `./tui` entry |

A `Host` profile holds what differs between hosts: the host's name in messages, how access is labelled, and notes shown above a tool's agents. Core builds the plugin from it with `createToolInspectorTui`. Core has no runtime dependency on either host; its sources are typed against `@opencode-ai/plugin`, and the Kilo package adapts Kilo's API type to them.

Shared tooling (TypeScript, ESLint, Prettier and the test runner) lives at the root. Tests live with the package they test: core's shared logic in `packages/core/tests`, and each host's output, baseline and packed-package tests in its own `tests` folder. The release workflow tests are in the root `tests` folder.

Core's package export is its TypeScript source, which npm links into the workspace's `node_modules`, so unit tests and typechecking run against it without a build.

Each host package builds with [tsdown](https://tsdown.dev) from its `tsdown.config.ts`: one ESM file and one declaration file per export (`dist/tui.js` and `dist/tui.d.ts`), for Node 22.18, unminified. The build inlines core, JavaScript and types, and keeps every other import external: the host's plugin types and `@opentui/core`, which the host maps to its own copy. `deps.onlyBundle` makes the build fail if anything from `node_modules` would be inlined, and `deps.onlyImport` makes it fail if the output imports any other package. Tool Inspector has one export per package, so nothing is split into shared chunks and module state such as core's caches exists once per host package. No host package lists core in any dependency field; a runtime dependency added to core must also be added to each host package's `dependencies` and to `deps.onlyImport` in both `tsdown.config.ts` files, since the bundle imports it, and the baseline and package tests that assert the host packages have no dependencies must be updated.

## Build local packages

Use the committed npm lockfile and run commands from the repository root. CI uses Node 24; the packages require Node 22.18 or later.

```sh
npm ci
npm run build
npm pack --workspace packages/opencode --workspace packages/kilo
```

This writes a tarball for each host package, with core bundled in. Install the host's tarball into a separate directory and register that installed package's absolute directory in the host's `tui.jsonc`. This exercises a local candidate without publishing it.

## Package shape

Both host packages are TUI-only. They export `./tui` and no root or `./server` entry, because OpenCode and Kilo load a package's root export as a server plugin.

## Checks

| Command | Coverage |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run check` | Typechecking, lint, formatting and unit tests for every package |
| `npm run test:package` | Each host package's tarball installed on its own outside the workspace: core bundled in and not installed, only the expected imports left external, the TUI export and its declarations |
| `npm run test:native` | The packed Kilo package in a real Kilo CLI TUI: live APIs, filtering, details, paging, Escape and repeated opens |

`npm run test:native` runs the native check for the host in `NATIVE_HOST`, which defaults to `kilo`; OpenCode has no native check. `KILO_TEST_VERSION` picks the Kilo CLI version: `floor` (the default), `latest-compatible` (the newest in the supported range) or an exact version. Set `KILO_BIN` to reuse an existing binary; its version is checked. The check installs the CLI and the packed package in temporary state and uses a loopback-only model fixture without sending prompts or running tools. It runs on Linux x64, under `script` from util-linux, and Windows x64, under a ConPTY from `node-pty`, which it installs beside the CLI.

Tests should protect observable behavior, safety boundaries and host contracts. The [shared standards](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/.github/blob/main/agent-guidance/common.md#meaningful-tests) define the testing policy.

## Host compatibility

Each host package keeps its supported range and floor in its tests folder: [packages/opencode/tests/opencode.json](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/blob/main/packages/opencode/tests/opencode.json) and [packages/kilo/tests/kilo.json](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/blob/main/packages/kilo/tests/kilo.json).

| Host | Plugin and SDK dev dependencies | `@opentui/*` | `solid-js` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OpenCode 1.19.x | `@opencode-ai/plugin`, `@opencode-ai/sdk` 1.19.5 | 0.4.5 | 1.9.12 |
| Kilo CLI 7.8.x | `@kilocode/plugin`, `@kilocode/sdk` 7.8.27 | 0.5.11 | 1.9.12 |

Each host's plugin and SDK dev dependencies share one exact version inside its range. Its `@opentui/*` and `solid-js` dev dependencies stay on the versions the host bundles, because the host maps a plugin's imports of them to its own copies. npm installs Kilo's OpenTUI copies under `packages/kilo/node_modules`, and Kilo's typecheck pins them with `paths` in `packages/kilo/tsconfig.json`. Core is typed against OpenCode's plugin types, so `npm run typecheck` also checks core's source against Kilo's through `packages/kilo/tsconfig.core.json`, which maps `@opencode-ai/plugin` to `@kilocode/plugin` and OpenTUI to Kilo's copies. Each package's baseline test enforces its pins against the lockfile, so update them only together with the supported range. Core's host dev dependencies match the OpenCode package's. No host runtime engine restriction is declared.

Other dependencies use version ranges, and `package-lock.json` decides what CI installs. Shared tooling at the root uses `^`, except TypeScript and Prettier, which use `~` because their minor releases change type checking and formatting. Third-party runtime dependencies use `^`. The exact pins are the host-matched dev dependencies above, the `node-pty` version the native check installs, and the npm version in the Release workflow's publish job.

[Check CI](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/blob/main/.github/workflows/check.yml) runs the unit and package tests on Linux and Windows for every pull request and push to `main`, and the static checks on Linux. Its native matrix runs the Kilo check on Linux and Windows, against the floor and the latest compatible Kilo CLI.

# Publishing

The [Release workflow](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/blob/main/.github/workflows/release.yml) runs only when started by hand on `main`, and publishes only when its **publish** input is checked. One run releases the version the two host packages share:

- `@lunchbox-labs/opencode-tool-inspector`
- `@lunchbox-labs/kilo-tool-inspector`

Core (`packages/core`) is private: each package's build bundles it in, so it is never packed or published. The run publishes the packages to npm in that order, creates the `v<version>` tag on the release commit, and publishes a GitHub release for that tag with the two package tarballs attached and notes generated from the merged pull requests. Branch pushes, pull requests and tag pushes do not publish packages.

## Publisher setup

The workflow expects these settings, configured through the respective services. This page describes the required setup, not confirmation of its current state.

- **npm trusted publishers:** one for each of the two packages, each with organization `lunchbox-labs`, repository `tool-inspector-plugin`, workflow filename `release.yml` and environment `release`. Allow direct `npm publish`, which is the command this workflow uses. `@lunchbox-labs/opencode-tool-inspector` already has one; `@lunchbox-labs/kilo-tool-inspector` needs its own before its first release, as [Bootstrap a new package](#bootstrap-a-new-package) describes. See [npm's trusted publishing guide](https://docs.npmjs.com/trusted-publishers/).
- **`release` environment:** allows deployments from `main` only. It holds no secrets or variables.
- **Actions policy:** only maintainers may start Release, and Wiki may run only on pushes to `main`. Both can write to the repository.
- **Tag rulesets:** a ruleset blocks updating and deleting `v*` tags. No ruleset blocks creating them, because Release creates the tag itself.

The publish job has `id-token: write` for OIDC and `contents: read`. It installs a trusted-publishing-capable npm version and enables provenance. The workflow does not use a long-lived npm token. Only the GitHub release job has `contents: write`, and it runs no repository code. Both jobs run in the `release` environment.

## Bootstrap a new package

npm adds a trusted publisher only to a package that already exists, and Release stops at verification while either package has never been published. `@lunchbox-labs/kilo-tool-inspector` was added in 0.3.0 and needs this once before its first Release run; `@lunchbox-labs/opencode-tool-inspector` is already on npm:

1. Publish a placeholder by hand, signed in to npm as a maintainer of the `lunchbox-labs` organization. Work in an empty directory outside this repository with only a minimal `package.json`, not the built package, so the placeholder has no code or dependencies:

   ```sh
   mkdir bootstrap && cd bootstrap
   echo '{}' > package.json
   npm pkg set name=@lunchbox-labs/kilo-tool-inspector version=0.0.0-bootstrap.0 license=MIT description="Placeholder; install a released version" repository.type=git repository.url=git+https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin.git repository.directory=packages/kilo
   npm publish --access public --tag bootstrap
   ```

2. Mark the placeholder as deprecated, so an install of it says what to use instead: `npm deprecate @lunchbox-labs/kilo-tool-inspector@0.0.0-bootstrap.0 "Placeholder; install a released version"`.
3. In the package's settings on npm, add the trusted publisher described above.
4. Run Release with **publish** unchecked to confirm verification passes, then run it again with **publish** checked.

npm points `latest` at a package's first version whatever tag it was published under, so `latest` names the placeholder until the first stable release moves it; a pre-release run publishes under `next` and leaves `latest` on the placeholder. `npm dist-tag ls <package>` shows where each tag points. Release refuses `0.0.0` and its pre-releases, the placeholder included, so a release can't collide with it.

The check in Verify covers only packages that are missing from npm. It can't tell whether a trusted publisher is set up, and a run without **publish** stops before the publish job, so it doesn't exercise OIDC either. A missing or wrong trusted publisher fails Publish npm at that package, after the packages before it were published. Fix the trusted publisher, then re-run only the failed jobs within the artifact's three days: Publish npm skips the packages npm already holds with the same tarball and publishes the rest.

Core is not published. If a placeholder of `@lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-core` was ever published while it was planned as a package, leave it deprecated; nothing installs it.

## Prepare and run a release

1. Set the same version in `packages/opencode/package.json` and `packages/kilo/package.json` (and in `packages/core/package.json` to keep them aligned; Release doesn't read core's), and run `npm install` so the package entries in `package-lock.json` match. Use a non-placeholder semantic version that has no tag and neither package has on npm yet: a stable version such as `1.2.3` for a release, or a pre-release version such as `1.2.3-beta.1` for a pre-release.
2. Complete the required checks and review, and integrate the release commit into `main` through the repository's normal process.
3. Open **Actions**, choose **Release**, and select **Run workflow** with `main` as the branch and **publish** checked. The run releases the commit at the head of `main` when it starts, so start it once the release commit is the latest commit there. Run it once per version.

The run has two inputs:

- **publish:** off by default. Unchecked, the run builds, checks and packs the release and keeps the tarballs only as the run's `release` artifact, then stops before npm, the tag and the GitHub release. It still stops at Verify when the version is already tagged or on npm. Check it to publish the official release.
- **prerelease:** publishes under npm's `next` tag instead of `latest`, and marks the GitHub release as a pre-release. A pre-release run needs a pre-release version, and a normal run a stable one, so `latest` never moves to a pre-release.

The run's summary names the version as soon as the **Release version** job finishes, and links the release once the **GitHub release** job has published it. Don't push the tag or create the release by hand: Release refuses a version that is already tagged, and tags can't be moved or deleted.

## What the run does

**Release version** stops a run started on any other branch, reads the version from the two packages and stops unless they have the same one. **Verify** then requires the checked-out commit to match the run's commit, stops when either package has never been published (see [Bootstrap a new package](#bootstrap-a-new-package)), and stops before building when `v<version>` is already tagged or either package already has that version on npm. [validate-release.mjs](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/blob/main/scripts/validate-release.mjs) also validates each package's identity, repository, registry, access, that it doesn't list core in any dependency field, and its lockfile entry. Verify runs `npm ci` and `npm run test:package`, packs the two builds and uploads the tarballs with SHA-256 checksums.

**Check** runs the [Check workflow](https://github.com/lunchbox-labs/tool-inspector-plugin/blob/main/.github/workflows/check.yml) on the release commit as part of the run, with every job it runs on a push to `main`. Its runs inside Release are grouped apart from Check's own runs, so a push to `main` during a release doesn't cancel them.

**Publish npm** downloads the verified tarballs, checks their checksums and publishes them in order, OpenCode first, with scripts disabled. It does not rebuild the packages. **GitHub release** then creates the `v<version>` tag on the release commit and publishes a GitHub release for it with the same two tarballs attached.

If a job fails, inspect it before retrying, and re-run only the failed jobs so the verified packages are reused. Re-running Publish npm is safe: it skips each package npm already holds at this version with the same tarball, publishes the rest, and stops at a package npm holds with a different tarball. Re-running GitHub release accepts an existing tag only on the release commit, publishes a draft left for the tag with the tarballs attached, and leaves an already published release as it is. A new run, or a full re-run, stops at verification once the version is tagged or any package is on npm, so finish a partly failed release by re-running its failed jobs within the artifact's three days. After that, bump the version, merge it to `main` and run Release again. Keep release-specific investigation and validation evidence in the tracking issue.

# Usage

Tool Inspector is a TUI plugin that lists the tools the host offers a model. It requires Node 22.18+. The OpenCode package is built for OpenCode 1.19.x, starting at 1.19.0, and the Kilo package for Kilo CLI 7.8.x, starting at 7.8.27. Both behave the same apart from the differences noted on this page.

## Install

Add the package for your host to `plugin` in `tui.jsonc`. The hosts keep their global configuration in separate folders: `~/.config/opencode/` for OpenCode and `~/.config/kilo/` for Kilo.

OpenCode:

```jsonc
{ "plugin": ["@lunchbox-labs/opencode-tool-inspector"] }
```

Kilo:

```jsonc
{ "plugin": ["@lunchbox-labs/kilo-tool-inspector"] }
```

Tool Inspector reads no environment variables or settings of its own. The host's own settings, such as `model`, `permission` and `experimental.primary_tools`, decide what it shows.

## Browse tools

Run `/tools`, or **Browse tools** from the command palette, to list the tools the host offers a model: the one the current session's latest message used, otherwise your configured `model`, otherwise the first connected provider's default. The dialog's title names the model and where it came from. If you switch models before your next prompt, the tools offered may differ.

Type to filter the list, and press Enter to see a tool's input schema, the agents that can use it and its full description. Escape returns to the list.

The list includes built-in and plugin tools. MCP server tools aren't listed, because the host only adds them when it runs a prompt; a toast says so when an MCP server is connected. If the host can't resolve tools for a model, the list shows tool names only.

## Input schema

The input shows each field's type, whether it's required, its allowed values, default and limits, with nested objects shown under their parent and each option of a union listed with its own fields. A definition the schema shares between fields, or one that contains itself, is listed once, and later uses say where its fields are. A reference to a definition the schema doesn't contain shows as unresolved, and one that takes more than 64 references in a row to reach a schema shows as a reference chain too long. Long enums, tuples and unions name their first few values and count the rest, and a schema too large to show in full is cut short with a note.

## Agent access

The tool list isn't filtered by agent. Instead, a tool's detail lists each agent and whether it's allowed to use the tool, asks first, is denied, or isn't offered the tool at all, following each agent's merged `permission` rules and the rules of the current top-level session. Input patterns with different access, such as `read` asking first for `*.env` files, are listed under the agent.

Agents with mode `all` also show their access when they run as a subagent, where that differs, since the host always denies subagents any `experimental.primary_tools`, and denies `todowrite` and `task` unless the agent's own rules name them.

The host's own hidden agents, such as `compaction` and `title`, are left out. If the host's agents can't be read, details open without the agents section and a toast says why.

### In Kilo

Kilo applies more checks at call time than its configured rules show, so the Kilo package words access as configured: "allowed by configured rules", "asks first by configured rules" and "denied by configured rules". Every tool's agents section starts with a note that Kilo can still ask or deny at call time, and that saved approvals, hard limits, skill commands and sandbox escalation aren't resolved here. Tools checked as `read` or `edit` add a note that Kilo checks protected config paths, such as sensitive `.env` files, separately, and `agent_manager` adds a note that its prompt, stop, move and answer actions need exact action rules. Headless subagent restrictions aren't shown either.
